items.why: Affects insurance audit compliance and claim settlement procedures for flood-affected clients.

items.summary: Nepal Insurance Authority has issued a brief procedure for settling insurance claims related to property, projects, and human casualties affected by the floods on August 27, 2023, along rivers including Lhende, Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani. It outlines requirements for surveyors, documents needed for motor and property/project claims, advance payments up to 50% of estimated liabilities, and timelines for settlement. Insurers and claimants affected by the 2023 floods in the specified regions must comply with these guidelines.
items.why: Provides essential procedures and documentation guidelines for auditing and settling specific disaster-related insurance claims.

items.summary: The Nepal Insurance Authority has issued a circular to all life and micro-life insurers to control mis-selling and misleading promotions. Insurers and agents are prohibited from selling insurance policies as fixed deposit or investment plans, making false promises of returns, or using unapproved promotional materials. Additionally, insurers must maintain records of mis-selling complaints and submit quarterly reports to the Authority.
items.why: Affects compliance and audit evidence for insurance sector audits.

items.title: According to the Insurance Act 2079, the insurance nature of the business need to be registered in Nepal Insurance Authority.
items.title_en: Insurance Business Registration Mandate Under Insurance Act 2079
items.summary: According to the Insurance Act 2079, entities cannot conduct insurance, reinsurance, or insurance-fund-related business without obtaining a license from the Nepal Insurance Authority under Section 24 and Section 153. Unauthorized insurance business operations by non-insurers will be treated as an insurance offense under Section 140(1)(a) and penalized under Section 141(1). This notice affects all organized institutions, firms, and companies using insurance-related terminology or conducting unauthorized insurance transactions.
items.why: Crucial for compliance regarding unauthorized insurance-related business names and transactions.

This follows the mandatory implementation of Nepal Standards on Quality Management (NSQM) effective from Shrawan 1, 2083. The soft copy of the guide is available on the ICAN website.
items.why: New NSQM 1-based Quality Management Policy Guide is mandatory for audit firms.

All affected members and firms can access and download the softcopy of this updated procedure from the Laws/Legislation tab under Members and Firm on the ICAN website. No specific deadlines, rates, or section numbers are mentioned in the notice.
items.why: Updated firm registration procedures affect CA and RA practice firm compliance.

items.title: Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) सम्बन्धी OTP मोबाइल नम्बरमा मात्र प्राप्त हुने सम्बन्धी सूचना ।
items.title_en: Notice Regarding UDIN OTP Sent Exclusively to Registered Mobile Number
items.summary: Starting from 2083/04/01, the One Time Password (OTP) for the Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) will be sent exclusively to the mobile number registered in ICAN's ERP system, rather than to both the mobile number and email. This change affects all professional members issuing professional reports. Consequently, members will no longer receive UDIN-related OTPs via email after this date.
items.why: UDIN OTP delivery is now restricted exclusively to the ICAN ERP registered mobile number.

items.title: Notice Regarding COP Upgrading of Registered Auditor Members
items.title_en: Notice Regarding COP Upgrading of Registered Auditor Members
items.summary: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal (ICAN) has upgraded the Certificate of Practice (COP) for certain registered auditor members based on their educational qualifications and experience, pursuant to Section 30(kha) of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1997 and Rule 4(2) of the Nepal Chartered Accountants Rules, 2004. The affected members are required to submit their original Certificate of Practice and firm registration certificates to the Institute in order to collect their new certificates. A list of 11 members upgraded from class 'Gha' to 'Ga' has been published.
items.why: Notice impacts qualifying registered auditors upgrading their Certificate of Practice.

items.title: Notice Advanced Management and Communication Skills (AMCS) Training
items.title_en: Notice Advanced Management and Communication Skills (AMCS) Training

Eligible CA CAP III and AT students must complete their registration by 24 August 2026 for a fee of NPR 26,000. Successful completion of this 15-day training is a mandatory requirement prior to applying for Institute membership.

The manual serves as a practical reference for Chartered Accountants and valuation practitioners across the country. It is available for download on the ICAN website under the Laws/Legislation section.
items.why: New Valuation Manual 2083 provides mandatory standards for valuation practice.

All professional accounting firms and members are affected by this update. The soft copy of the guideline can be accessed on the ICAN website under the Laws/Legislation tab within the Members and Firm section.
items.why: New guidelines govern the merger procedures for professional accounting firms.

The training costs NPR 3,000 (exclusive of VAT), and participating members will be awarded 20 CPE Credit Hours. Interested members are required to register through the provided online link.

items.title: NKP ११४९७ · Applicability of Customs Duty Rates at the Time of Goods Clearance
items.summary: The dispute concerned the correct timing and rate for levying customs duty on goods imported into Nepal. The Supreme Court held that customs duty is applicable based on the prevailing law at the time of clearance when goods are inspected and permitted to be removed from the customs premises, rather than when they first arrive. This decision turned on the legal provisions governing customs duties and clearance procedures.

items.summary: This case concerns whether failure to repay a bank loan or subsequent repayment constitutes a banking offense under the Banking Offense and Punishment Act. items.summary: The dispute involved whether expenses incurred by a company for training, seminars, and conferences to promote business can be taxed as casual gains. items.title: NKP ११३२८ · Tax Withholding on Retirement Fund Payments and Employment Income
items.summary: The Supreme Court addressed whether payments from an approved retirement fund are subject to withholding tax as employment income. The Court held that retirement fund payments are lump-sum final payments made upon retirement rather than monthly salary, and therefore cannot be treated or taxed as regular employment income under the Income Tax Act. The decision turned on the Income Tax Act, 2058 (specifically sections 8 and 63), the Income Tax Rules, 2059, and the Finance Act.
items.why: The Supreme Court addressed whether payments from an approved retirement fund are subject to withholding tax as employment income

The Court held that deducting 15 percent tax on amounts built from employee contributions violates the constitutional right to social security and that section 88(1) of the Income Tax Act cannot be interpreted to apply a 15 percent deduction on such contributory retirement payments. The case turned on the Income Tax Act, 2058 and the Income Tax Rules, 2059.

items.title: NKP ९९६७ · VAT credit eligibility on vehicles purchased for industrial business operations
items.summary: The issue was whether an industry could claim a Value Added Tax (VAT) credit on vehicles purchased for its business operations. The Supreme Court held that taxpayers are entitled to deduct VAT paid on vehicles necessary for and used in business operations, and authorities cannot deny this statutory benefit using general technical arguments. The case turned on the Value Added Tax Act.

items.title: NKP ९९२४ · Bank Manager's Liability in Letter of Credit and Customs Declaration Verification
items.summary: The issue was whether a bank manager and employees can be held liable for corruption when processing Letters of Credit (LC) without properly verifying customs documents, resulting in financial loss to the government. The Court held that commercial banks must strictly follow Nepal Rastra Bank directives, verify the authenticity of customs stamps and signatures on declaration forms, and failure resulting in government loss constitutes a corrupt act. The judgment turned on the rules, directives, and circulars issued by Nepal Rastra Bank regarding banking and foreign currency transactions.

items.summary: The issue was whether the Customs Department is legally bound to renew a bonded warehouse license and grant tax and custom duty facilities when the renewal application was not made within the time and procedure prescribed by law. The Court held that the licensee must fulfill statutory conditions and procedures to claim such facilities, and merely filing an application without following the due process does not compel the authorities to renew it. The case turned on the provisions of the relevant Economic Ordinances and Economic Acts concerning customs and licensing procedures.

items.title: NKP ९८०९ · Distinction Between Company and Shareholders Under Company Act
items.summary: The plaintiff filed a case seeking cancellation of share transfer pursuant to an agreement. The Supreme Court held that a company, its shareholders, promoters, and directors are legally distinct entities based on the principles of separate legal personality and limited liability. The case turned on the principles embodied in the Company Act, 2063.

items.title: NKP ९७५२ · Corporate Governance and Fiduciary Duties of Company Directors
items.summary: The case addressed allegations of corruption involving the leasing of company stalls below market value and subleasing them at higher rates. The Court held that directors act as trustees and agents of the company, owing a strict fiduciary duty of utmost good faith, and cannot engage in self-dealing or abuse minority shareholders' rights. The judgment turned on principles under the Companies Act regarding corporate governance, directors' duties, and corruption laws applicable to public institutions.
items.why: The case addressed allegations of corruption involving the leasing of company stalls below market value and subleasing them at higher rates

items.title: NKP ९७३६ · Challenge Against Minimum Audit Fee Fixation by ICAN
items.summary: The issue was whether the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal (ICAN) could unilaterally fix minimum audit service fees, restricting contractual freedom. The Supreme Court held that while ICAN can issue guidelines for service standards and quality, unilaterally fixing mandatory minimum fees without allowing contractual autonomy and consumer interests is not lawful. The decision turned on the Contract Act, 2056 and the governing professional acts.
items.why: The issue was whether the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal (ICAN) could unilaterally fix minimum audit service fees, restricting contractual freedom

items.title: NKP ९७०२ · Succession of Liabilities by a Newly Named Casino Company
items.summary: The issue was whether a newly registered casino company could evade the tax and employee liabilities of its predecessor entity through a mere change of name and registration. The Supreme Court held that a company which in substance continues the operations, assets, and liabilities of a predecessor using the same physical location and infrastructure cannot escape prior liabilities simply due to a change in name and form. The decision turned on general principles of company law regarding corporate identity and continuity.

items.summary: The issue was whether the Nepal Rastra Bank's directives and the subsequent bank decision to release collateral were lawful amidst borrower default and internal management disputes. The Court held that the borrower has a mandatory obligation to repay loans as agreed, and the Nepal Rastra Bank has the legal authority to issue necessary directives regarding loan recovery and collateral release. The case turned on the regulatory powers of Nepal Rastra Bank over banking and financial institutions.

items.title: NKP ९६५३ · Corruption in Building and Road Construction
items.summary: The Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority alleged corruption in tender evaluation and document falsification for building and road construction. The Supreme Court held that the evaluation committee properly followed procurement procedures and there was no evidence of illegal loss to the government or intentional wrongdoing by the officials. The case turned on the Public Procurement Act, 2063 and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 2059.

items.title: NKP ९६१३ · Levy of Forest Development Fund Fee Based on Directive
items.summary: The issue was whether the government could collect fees for the Forest Development Fund based merely on a directive rather than substantive law. The Supreme Court held that collecting taxes, fees, or charges without explicit authorization in a substantive Act violates constitutional principles. The judgment turned on Interim Constitution of Nepal, 2063 Article 89(1) and Income Tax Act, 2058 Section 2(ढ).
items.why: The issue was whether the government could collect fees for the Forest Development Fund based merely on a directive rather than substantive law

items.title: NKP ९६११ · Application of Income Tax and VAT Special Acts Over Revenue Leakage Act
items.summary: The Supreme Court held that regular tax non-compliance should be handled through specific tax collection mechanisms under special acts like the Income Tax Act and VAT Act, rather than arbitrarily invoking the Revenue Leakage (Investigation and Control) Act without evidence of tax evasion. It ruled that failure to file tax details is not automatically tax leakage, and search and seizure without sufficient justification is unjustified. The case primarily turned on the Income Tax Act and Value Added Tax Act.

items.title: NKP ९६०८ · Banking Offence and Violation of Nepal Rastra Bank Directives
items.summary: The issue was whether actions violating the Bank and Financial Institutions Act and Nepal Rastra Bank directives constitute a banking offence under the Banking Offence and Punishment Act. The Court held that violating regulatory directives does not automatically attract the Banking Offence and Punishment Act, and the prosecution failed to objectively prove the charges. The case turned on the Bank and Financial Institutions Act, 2063, the Banking Offence and Punishment Act, 2064, and the Evidence Act, 2031.

items.title: NKP ९५९६ · Writ against tax assessment dismissed due to alternative remedy of appeal
items.summary: The issue was whether a writ petition could be entertained against a tax office decision when an alternative remedy of appeal existed. The Court held that since the law provides a remedy of appeal to the Revenue Tribunal under the Income Tax Act, extraordinary writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked, bypassing the ordinary legal forum. This decision turned on section 116(1) of the Income Tax Act, 2058.
items.why: The issue was whether a writ petition could be entertained against a tax office decision when an alternative remedy of appeal existed

items.title: NKP ९५८१ · Cooling Period for Company Directors Appointed as Employees
items.summary: The issue was whether a former company director could immediately be appointed as an employee or advisor after leaving the board. The Court held that an ineligible person cannot be a candidate, and a one-year cooling period is required to prevent conflicts of interest, ensure good governance, and avoid undue advantage, drawing parallels to the Nepal Rastra Bank Act. This case turned on company law principles regarding governance and cooling periods.
items.why: The issue was whether a former company director could immediately be appointed as an employee or advisor after leaving the board

items.summary: The plaintiff filed a case seeking investment security and compensation regarding a joint investment dispute in a company where share distribution agreements were contested. The Court held that compensation cannot be awarded without establishing objective loss or bad faith, and that converting the company to a single shareholder through an extraordinary general meeting called pursuant to the Companies Act was lawful. The case turned on section 829(4) of the Companies Act, 2063.

items.summary: The prosecution alleged illegal acquisition of property and corruption against a civil servant and family members. The Supreme Court held that property registered in another person's name or bank account cannot be attributed to the defendant without making them a co-accused, and legal business transactions or tax-assessed incomes cannot be arbitrarily deemed illegal without proof. The case turned on the Prevention of Corruption Act, 2059.

items.summary: The issue was whether the Customs Office properly rejected the declared transaction value and determined a higher customs value without following statutory procedures. The case turned on Section 13(4) of the Customs Act, 2019 and Schedule 1, Section 7 of the Economic Ordinance, 2061.

items.summary: The issue was whether the Company (Electronic Filing) Directive, 2069 infringed constitutional rights by requiring online submissions. The Court held that the delegated legislation supported technological advancement, eased service delivery, and did not violate any rights. The case turned on Section 16(2) of the Companies Act, 2063.

items.title: NKP ९४९१ · Classification of Banks and Deposit Restrictions for State Entities
items.summary: Development bankers challenged statutory provisions requiring state entities and public funds to deposit monies only in commercial or 'A' class banks, claiming it violated their economic freedoms and equality rights. The Supreme Court held that 'A' and 'B' class financial institutions have different statutory statuses, scopes, and licensing conditions, and thus differing operational regulations do not violate equality rights or freedom of trade. The case turned on the Bank and Financial Institutions Act, 2063 and the Nepal Rastra Bank Act, 2058.

items.title: NKP ९४३० · Taxability of Undistributed Bonus Amounts under Income Tax
items.summary: The issue was whether an amount set aside for bonuses but not distributed in the subsequent year should be included in the company's net income for tax purposes. The Court held that bonus amounts set aside in the current year and not distributed in the following year must be calculated as part of the company's net income and become taxable. This decision turned on the Income Tax Act.
items.why: The issue was whether an amount set aside for bonuses but not distributed in the subsequent year should be included in the company's net income for tax purposes

items.summary: The Supreme Court considered whether an accused could be convicted of money laundering when found in possession of disproportionate assets without a legitimate source. The Court held that money laundering is a secondary offense where the burden of proof lies on the defendant to establish the lawful source of abnormal assets under section 28 of the Act. The case was ultimately referred to a full bench due to differing judicial opinions. The case turned on the Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2064, specifically sections 4 and 28.

The Court held that banks must follow Nepal Rastra Bank directives, respect loan agreements, consult customers before changing interest rates, and avoid arbitrary increases. The Supreme Court held that the writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked when an alternative remedy exists and has already been utilized, as doing so leads to judicial inconsistency. items.summary: The petitioner challenged a tax assessment order issued by the Tax Office based on delegated authority from the Tax Settlement Commission. The Supreme Court held that the power to assess tax cannot be delegated as it is a quasi-judicial power, and doing so violates the principles of justice and the purpose of the Commission. items.summary: The dispute concerned whether an industry registered before the publication of a restrictive notice is entitled to excise duty exemptions. The Court held that an industry is entitled to facilities and protections acquired under prevailing laws at the time of registration, which cannot be revoked by subsequent notices unless expressly restricted. This decision turned on section 10, clause (c), sub-clause (1) of the Industrial Enterprises Act, 2038.
